newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-MATIF outlines battle plan for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-MATIF outlines battle plan for EMU.

text.p: The French futures and options exchange MATIF on Wednesday outlined a battle plan for retaining a healthy slice of the futures market after the planned introduction of the single European currency, the euro, in 1999.

A report by a MATIF working committee recommended the launch of a euro-interest rate future, a five-year bond future and explored the practical difficulties of switching existing contracts into euro-denominated products.

Jacques Werren, MATIF deputy managing director, told a news conference he recognised the exchange's arch-rival, the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) had the upper hand in some areas, especially interest rate futures.
But he said all that could change when economic and monetary union (EMU) is launched in 1999, an event he likened to a Europewide "Big Bang".
MATIF was in a position to benefit substantially from the changeover, especially if a European money market developed alongside the London market.

"The European Monetary Union zone will become MATIF's domestic market base, an advantage to be exploited particularly at the short end of the yield curve so the Euro money market differentiates itself clearly from the London market," he said.

The committee said new benchmark short-term interest rates should be set up by a panel of 20 to 30 banks within the European single currency zone. This would create a "Euribor", or average inter-bank rate offered by EU banks to prime borrowers.

"Should the United Kingdom not join EMU, or should obligatory reserves be imposed on banks inside the EMU zone, the European money market could be divided between a continental and an offshore market, which would justify the existence of two distinct benchmarks," the report said.

The ailing European currency unit (Ecu) market received little comfort from the report. France is one of the few countries still trying to support the Ecu bond market, but the working group said it rejected the idea of launching any more Ecu derivative products.

"The members of the working committee have reservations about the future of the Ecu between now and 1999, and reject a priori a strategy based on developing a range of Ecu products on MATIF ahead of the transition to the euro," the report said.
At a conference organised by MATIF on Wednesday to discuss the move to a single currency, MATIF chairman Gerard Pfauwadel was in an upbeat mood.
"We are the only ones to be able to show today a coherent strategy for the switch to the euro," he said.

Werren said in the report that French government debt was ideally placed to become the benchmark for European interest rate markets, given its liquidity and the French commitment to converting debt into euros in January 1999.
The lone dissenting voice at the MATIF conference was Martin Hufner, chief economist at Bayerishce Vereinsbank, who said: "I don't think the competition is over yet."

He said he expected Germany to announce before the end of year it would convert its debt into euros in 1999, boost liquidity along the yield curve and create a Bund market that would allow interest payments to be separated from the underlying bond.
"I have the impression France is still ahead in adjusting market institutions to EMU. On the other hand in Germany private banks have been guiding the process," Hufner said.
